tour.title: Quick tour
tour.s1: Place the part on the screen, against the ruler's edge. Drag the round knobs so the thin lines touch the part's ends.
tour.s2: While dragging, a loupe shows the edge magnified. Hold a second finger anywhere for precision mode (handle moves at 1/10 speed).
tour.s3: Long-press a knob to set it as zero or type an exact value. Use Nudge for single-pixel steps.
tour.s4: Black part on a black screen? Tap the contrast button or open Background to pick the best colour automatically.
tour.s5: Tap Save to store the reading in a record with a photo. Lock freezes the tools while you place or remove the part.

welcome.tagline: A calibrated pocket metrology kit — honest about its accuracy, works offline.
welcome.step1: Mark the flat part of your screen (curved edges, notch).
welcome.step2: Calibrate with a bank/ID card or a steel rule.
welcome.step3: Measure, save with a photo, and keep records.
welcome.tip: Look straight down over the edge you are aligning. Place hard parts gently — they can scratch the screen.

cal.title: Calibration
cal.intro: Browsers do not know the physical size of your screen, so Maapak must be calibrated once against a real object.
cal.cardHint: Any ID-1 card: 85.60 × 53.98 mm. Fast, good accuracy.
cal.rulerHint: Align two lines to graduations as far apart as possible, on both axes.
cal.customHint: Align two lines to an object whose size you know.
cal.customAxisHint: Long axis gives a longer baseline and a smaller error.
cal.estimateInfo: Current estimate: about {{ppi}} device px per inch (from the browser's 160 px/inch rule). Not used as “Calibrated”.
cal.coinNote: Coin calibration is not offered yet: coin diameters must be verified against official mint data first, and India has several coin series in circulation.
cal.cardInstr: Put the card on the outline with its top and left edges on the two fixed black lines. Drag the coloured right line and bottom line exactly onto the card's edges (the loupe helps). Look straight down.
cal.rulerYInstr: Lay a steel rule along the long side. Align the two lines to two graduations as far apart as fit (e.g. 10 and 110), then enter the real distance.
cal.rulerXInstr: Now along the short side: align the two lines to two graduations and enter the distance. Or skip to use the same scale.
cal.customInstr: Align the two lines to the ends of your object and type its known size.
cal.verifyInstr: Verify: place the card again (long edge along the screen) with its top edge on the black line, and drag the coloured line to its bottom edge.
cal.enterDistance: Enter the real distance in mm
cal.enterSize: Enter the known size in mm
cal.axisWarn: The two axes differ by more than 1 %. Possible misalignment — repeat the calibration if this phone has square pixels.
cal.singleAxisNote: Only one axis was measured; the same scale is used for both (phone pixels are practically square).
cal.residualHigh: more than 0.3 mm off, recalibrating is suggested
cal.portraitOnly: Calibrate in portrait orientation. Rotate the phone upright.

accuracy.title: Accuracy statement
accuracy.body:
Every reading shows its expanded uncertainty U (≈95 %), for example ±0.3 mm. It combines pixel resolution, edge alignment, calibration error and parallax: u = √(u_res² + u_align² + (L·r_cal)² + u_par²), U = 2u rounded up.
The number of decimals follows U: you never see more digits than the phone can deliver.
Typical after card calibration on a ~400 ppi phone with the loupe: ±0.2–0.4 mm up to 100 mm.

calibration.title: Why calibrate?
calibration.body:
Browsers report CSS pixels, not millimetres; 1 CSS inch is not a real inch. Maapak stores device pixels per millimetre for each screen axis.
Card: quick and good. Steel rule over a long baseline: most accurate. Changing the browser zoom, Android “Display size”, the browser or the phone breaks the scale — Maapak detects this and disables measuring until you recalibrate.

parallax.title: Viewing angle (parallax)
parallax.body:
Pixels sit under the cover glass. Looking at 30° through 1 mm of glass shifts the line by about 0.4 mm. Tall parts are worse: aligning to the top of a 10 mm bolt head viewed at 20° is off by about 3.6 mm.
Look straight down over the edge, and align to the edge that touches the glass. Sighting lines extend beyond the part to help.

tools.title: Ruler modes
tools.body:
Ruler: single scale with two markers.
Gap: two parallel rulers — the gap is the width, the markers give the length (L × W in one setup).
Split: metric on top, inch below, shared cursor lines (or metric numbered from both ends).
Leapfrog: for parts longer than the screen — mark, move the phone, align zero to the mark, repeat; uncertainty grows as √N.
T-square: up to 4 rulers that snap parallel or at 90°.

shield.title: Ghost touches
shield.body: Metal parts on a capacitive screen can create phantom touches. Only touches that start on a handle move a tool; large contact areas (palm, part) are ignored. Use Lock while placing or removing the part.

limits.title: What a screen cannot measure
limits.body: Thickness and depth: the screen is 2D, so the caliper has no depth rod. Objects much larger than the screen need Leapfrog (or photo measurement in a later phase). The app cannot set screen brightness.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.body: No account and no analytics. Calibrations, records and photos are stored only in this browser on this device.

learn.caliperPrompt: Read the vernier and type your reading in {{unit}}.
learn.explain: Main scale {{main}} {{unit}} (last line before the vernier zero) + coinciding vernier line {{line}} × {{lc}} = {{reading}} {{unit}}

caliper.title: Vernier caliper
caliper.body:
Outside jaws (below the beam) measure OD, length and width; the small inside jaws (above) measure ID of a ring or hole lying flat. Read the main scale just before the vernier zero, then find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main-scale line: reading = main + line × least count.
Least counts: 0.1 mm (10 lines over 9 mm), 0.05 mm (20 over 39 mm), 0.02 mm (50 over 49 mm), 0.001″ (25 over 0.600″).
There is no depth rod: a screen cannot measure depth. The digital value always follows the honest-decimals rule, even if the vernier shows 0.02 mm.

tol.title: Tolerance for {{label}}
tol.hint: Green: inside the limits by more than the uncertainty. Amber: within the uncertainty of a limit (not certain). Red: out.
